articles.fullContent: OpenAI和Anthropic等大型人工智能实验室已将赌注押在提供聊天机器人上，这些聊天机器人具备专门功能，能够回答与健康相关的问题。 苹果公司正在开展一项新研究，以了解人们如何使用人工智能来管理健康。 但它目前还没有完全跟上其他人工智能初创公司的步伐；它希望研究基于临床的答案如何能够帮助人们。 这家iPhone制造商正在与专注于医疗保健的人工智能公司OpenEvidence合作，推出一款新的研究应用程序。 苹果正在邀请符合以下条件的用户参与：年满21周岁、居住在美国、使用iPhone 15或更新机型、运行iOS 26或更新版本，且已启用Apple Intelligence。 该公司计划在12个月以上的时间里开展这项研究，参与者人数最多可达20万人。 这款新应用将允许用户像使用ChatGPT或Claude一样提出与健康相关的问题，答案将基于来自《新英格兰医学杂志》、《美国医学会杂志》和《自然》等来源的临床数据。 苹果表示，该应用程序将尝试对日常医疗问题给出简明扼要的答案。 用户可以对这些答案进行评分，并提供有关回复的反馈；他们还会被要求参与每月调查。 参与者可以分享HealthKit中的数据，例如静息心率、活动、睡眠或实验室结果，以便从应用程序中获得更个性化、更有针对性的建议。 该公司表示，该应用程序还可以帮助参与者更好地为看医生做好准备，并将引导用户找到具体的医疗服务提供者，以获得与相关医疗问题有关的答案。 苹果公司明确表示，数据在发送到安全的第三方云提供商之前将进行匿名处理，且不会用于训练任何类型的人工智能模型。 该公司表示，OpenEvidence会在24小时后删除查询和回复数据。 “在苹果，我们认为负责任的创新始于科学严谨和临床基础。 健康具有深刻的个人性，开展专门的研究是了解人们在日常生活中如何接触、理解和评估健康人工智能的最周全方式。”——Sumbul Desai医学博士 苹果公司健康与健身副总裁在声明中表示，并补充道：“这项研究的洞见将有助于推动更广泛的科学讨论，并确保随着技术的发展，我们继续打造值得信赖的工具，真正为人们的健康之旅提供支持，无论他们身处何方。” 从今天起，美国用户可以下载该应用程序。 目前尚不清楚苹果是否希望在其“健康”应用或Siri中推出由人工智能驱动的问答功能。 其潜力巨大——今年早些时候，OpenAI表示，用户每周提出的与健康相关的问题超过3亿个。 如果您通过我们文章中的链接进行购买，我们可能会赚取少量佣金。 这不会影响我们的编辑独立性。 Ivan在TechCrunch报道全球消费科技的发展动态。

articles.fullContent: 我们没有预料到会发生这种情况。 或者至少我没有预料到——一周前，当我写到英伟达董事会对当时的首席执行官黄仁勋展开调查时，我以为他的职位是稳固的。 在TechCrunch的Equity播客最新一期节目中，Rebecca Bellan、Tim De Chant和我讨论了黄仁勋是如何被罢免的，以及这对更广阔的人工智能经济意味着什么。 虽然蒂姆表示他预料到会发生这种情况（尽管没有这么快），但丽贝卡说：“我根本没想到会发生这种情况。” “Jensen就是Nvidia，对吧？”她补充道。 “而且这个经济体有很大一部分都依赖于英伟达。” 同样，我也对黄仁勋的支持似乎如此迅速地崩塌感到惊讶，每天似乎都有更多的丑闻曝出。 （与此同时，仍有许多人希望看到他回归。 ）我们还花了一些时间思考Nvidia在更广阔的人工智能生态系统中的投资将走向何方。 请继续阅读，以预览我们的对话（为篇幅和清晰起见进行了编辑）；您可以在此处收听完整的一期节目。 Tim De Chant：我就知道会有这么一天。 我没想到会这么快发生。 我以为至少还会过几天。 Rebecca Bellan：我根本没想到会发生这样的事。 我的意思是，Jensen就是Nvidia，对吧？ 而这个经济体有很大一部分都依赖于Nvidia。 我们只有过去几年的数据，这些数据向我们表明，亿万富翁可以为所欲为。 所以他的辞职让我感到很惊讶 — 这几乎让我重拾了对人性的信心。 但有人对我说：“如果这是埃隆，什么都不会发生。” 他不会辞职的。 什么都不会发生。Anthony Ha：这很有趣，因为要是一周前，甚至仅仅是几天前，我都会说Jensen与Elon属于同一类人。 我的意思是，没有人像埃隆那样特别，但它是一家规模庞大、极其成功的公司。 正如您所说，在很多方面，整个人工智能经济都是建立在Nvidia的基础之上。 对于大多数人来说，黄仁勋就是英伟达。 他是最大的股东。 他的家人在公司工作，也许最重要的是，公司没有制定继任计划。 所以，他们对此完全没有准备。 Rebecca：我认为我们实际上应该退后一步，因为我们刚刚开始这场谈话，就理所当然地认为我们的听众会知道我们在说什么。 但对于那些不知情的人来说，在传出Jensen与Nvidia客户Megaspeed的一名前高管有染后，他于周四辞职。该前高管据称与中国情报部门有联系。 然后还有一桩据称与英伟达高管的婚外情。

articles.rawFullText: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman . That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely . But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere . This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair . Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube , where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder . Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth. What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years. Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff? Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment. The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way. In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close. There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective. I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.” With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day. This is just off the top of my head, not as a researcher, but my understanding is the people in these spaces say, “We could do so, so, so much.” They could do that if you just had a magic wand and waved it and said, “Everyone freeze on the new capability side and just let these people do their thing.” Again, if you’re just having a higher bar for how confident we need to be that the risk is being managed reasonably, then that would also create space and incentives for more of that work to be done as it’s needed for new training and releases. One idea that I’ve heard you talk about in the past is that maybe we should just restrict training and say the models are good enough right now. They have not diffused into society and we should just use all the compute for inference and let everyone figure out what the AI is for. That’ll generate a bunch of money and hopefully use that money to improve safety. Do you think that’s a realistic policy proposal? I wouldn’t go for that black-and-white a version of “no more training, only inference,” but I do think that there’s… this isn’t my framing, but I like it. I think this idea of decelerating the vertical growth of AI, meaning the pure capabilities growth, making more and more and more advanced AI models, but trying to accelerate the horizontal growth, meaning integrating AI into different use cases, fine-tuning models that could solve specific problems, integrating it into parts of the economy that might take longer, and solving scientific problems. Sometimes people talk about wanting to slow down AI and they mean just the very specific thing of slowing down the growth of the most advanced models, but people sometimes take them to mean slowing down everything to do with AI. So less deployment, less experimentation, less integration, which I think would be a much worse idea. You asked if it is feasible, I think. Well, is that just a good path? If we could put a bill in front of our new Congress and the bill said, “Stop spending all the money on training and put all your resources on safety.” Part of that is, “Sure, let it rip on inference. More and more industries will figure out what AI is good for and not good for. Some bad things will happen, but we will focus your profits on fixing the things for now.” There’s a policy idea embedded in there that is workable. The implementation might be very challenging, but it’s a workable policy idea. Actually, I’ll give you an example that I’ve been thinking about as we’ve been talking. We just had Bill Gates on the show , and I tried to do the same exercise with him. What is the nature of the technology? What is the nature of the companies? Do you think it’s alive? Basically, his response, the sum total of that hour I spent with him, was, “Who cares? The problem is now.” I would ask him, “What is the nature of AI?” And he’s like, “I don’t give a shit. Everything’s going to get ruined. Do something.” That’s just been swirling in my head as we’ve been talking. So one workable policy solution is “don’t use the computer chips for that , use the computer chips for this . That’s going to create a bunch of problems and necessarily we will have to create safety thresholds and all the other stuff.” And then you can go make the next generation of models that are even more powerful and we’ll have some muscles. We’ll have some capability to deal with it. It just doesn’t seem like the industry is going to come to that conclusion on its own. It’s a pretty heavy hammer. I don’t feel like it’s what we need today, but I do think it’s the kind of thing that I could imagine working. Again, if the OpenAI and Anthropic people are right and we only have two years before the god machine, then I think we’re going to have a number more steps in the pipeline of people getting freaked out and people wanting to do something about it. I think if we are seeing models that are agents and systems that are getting more and more capable and wreaking more and more havoc, then that is certainly the shape of things that could make sense. My last question in this phase is what to make of these companies. We’ve been talking about the technology in a very abstract way. If I read Anthropic’s S-1, one very obvious conclusion is they should stop training new models. They should just start selling the very lucrative inference tokens they have today and the technology is not diffused into the market and probably some competitor should come along and be like, “I’ve distilled a version of Claude and I’m going to run around every local plumbing business in America and do whatever automation I can for lots and lots of money.” That is a market dynamic that may occur or may not. But Dario wants to build AGI. There’s not a market dynamic that’s going to stop him from that. Yeah, he really does. He really, really does. You obviously have insight into all these companies. What do we make of the companies? Are they single-minded in purpose? Are they all doomers? Are they going to stop themselves? I heard you had Kevin Roose on your podcast recently , and I think I would echo something that I heard him saying there, which I forget if he said it explicitly or if I just extrapolated it in my head, which is basically there’s this sort of AGI-pilled mindset. There’s this mindset that the systems that we have today are not fundamentally very far away from systems that could be incredibly, incredibly powerful. That’s the direction things are going in and that’s the direction we should maybe want them to go in so that you’re building AGI. Building AGI is feasible and we could do it soon and the systems we have are not far away. That was this crazy, heretical, “get you laughed out of the room” kind of view in 2016 or 2017, and even before that, right? DeepMind, when it was founded in 2010, was an AGI company and at the time it was like, “Wow, what a bunch of weirdos.” The same thing was true of OpenAI when it was founded at the end of 2015. They were an AGI company and that was a very weird thing to say and a very weird thing to be. What we’ve seen over the past 10 years is that bunch of weirdos who had this weird belief that the AI systems we can build are not just great B2B SaaS products. They’re not just fun chatbots. They’re going to fundamentally change the nature of the universe. That group of people keeps being right in the sense of building the best AI systems that the most people want to use and that make the most money. I think you have that set of true believers — which is very concentrated in OpenAI and Anthropic, but there are also some of them at Google, Meta, and SpaceX — and they haven’t been right about everything, to be clear, but their star has risen. So you now have people who are not AGI-pilled feeling like they have to pander to those who are so that they can attract the good researchers who will build their good B2B SaaS products. But if you’re just saying AGI-pilled things so that you can hire the researchers to build the B2B SaaS, then you’re not actually going to get there. I do like the idea of the AGI-pilled, starry-eyed executive throwing off his coat and revealing that he was just a SaaS salesman all along. [Laughs] Yeah, I’m thinking of someone like Zuckerberg here. I don’t know him personally. Maybe he is more AGI-pilled than I think he is. Alexandr Wang is AGI-pilled. Absolutely. And so what did Zuckerberg have to do to get Alexandr Wang to believe? It seems like throwing him lots of money, both for his own salary and also to spend on his team. If you’re looking at these different companies, it makes sense to try and think about, “Okay, who here is AGI-pilled and who isn’t?” A fun dynamic, or a very irritating dynamic sitting in DC, is that all these companies, including the very AGI-pilled ones, have these lobbying arms, these government affairs arms, that are so not AGI-pilled. So you hear Sam or Dario or their top executives and top researchers talking about things. And then you go and sit in a closed-door roundtable in DC with their top policy or government affairs people, and it’s like night and day. They’re very much in the B2B SaaS mindset. People who come from the lobbying world, often their whole job is to make sure the government isn’t too worried about whatever your company is doing. It’s like, “We got it. We’re good,” which is often pretty jarring when you’re familiar with what their bosses are saying. One of the dynamics here that’s super fascinating is right now they’re weird research labs with lots of money and lobbyists talking to politicians, and there isn’t some countervailing economic pressure in their structures. They don’t have to make money, but soon Anthropic will go public. It’s funny you mentioned Kevin Roose. He is AGI-pilled and I’m not, so I think that’s a healthy dynamic for both of us to be friends. But he wrote in his book that Sam Altman leaving OpenAI and then coming back was when OpenAI changed forever. It stopped being a research lab and it started being a much more commercial entity that was actually chasing profits in some way. Indeed, OpenAI did restructure . I mean, you were in the middle of that. I’m curious, is that how you see it — that the industry has gotten more commercialized? To me, it fits into this long-running debate that has been happening in AI safety circles for 10 to 20 years: Is AGI, human-level AI or powerful AI or advanced AI or whatever, is that something where it’s going to go from something very small to suddenly being very powerful? Eliezer Yudkowsky will talk about “ foom ,” as in the takeoff, where you have this AI that’s not that great, but it figures out the right algorithm and then suddenly foom — it’s incredibly smart, incredibly fast. The other kind of take would be, “No, this is something that’s going to compound over time. It’s going to take a while to get from the less-advanced systems to the more-advanced systems and it’s going to be economically useful along the way.” So people are going to be building businesses around it. It’s going to take some time to ladder up. I think maybe it was literally Kevin on his episode with you talking about how there’s this Anthropic document from the early days where they say, “Oh, we’re only going to need 100 people or something in our lab.” That’s a very foom kind of idea: “We’re just going to need to do really good research and come up with the right ideas and then we’re going to suddenly have very, very advanced models.” Basically, I think what we’ve seen over the past four years since ChatGPT came out was that that turned out to be wrong. You had these research-focused and AGI-focused labs, and they still call themselves labs because they think of themselves as research groups that initially started selling API access as a way to fund the research. OpenAI did this, and Anthropic did this as well. It was kind of an accident that they started doing these consumer products. ChatGPT famously released as a research preview, not as a product. But it was so successful that these research labs that wanted to be doing research, that wanted to be focusing on the big ideas and on building the most event systems, had this accidental massive commercial success at the same time as they were realizing that they were going to need an enormous amount of capital to scale. The best research approaches that they could do didn’t involve being really smart and thoughtful and having great ideas. They involved having gigantic computing clusters that cost, at this point, hundreds of billions of dollars. This is a long way of saying, yes, I agree with you, they’ve become businesses, but I think it is not because they’ve gone through some mindset shift. I think it’s because the path of the tech tree that we’re going down both requires enormous amounts of capital and also is capable of generating enormous amounts of revenue because it is actually useful along the way. You see this in the fact that both OpenAI and Anthropic have gone this route, even though their management philosophies and research philosophies are quite different, that it’s an imperative that they both had to make the money and it was so easy for them to build enormously revenue-generating businesses because the tech was so useful long before it reached the point of machine god. So I think that’s a long way of agreeing with you, but with some extra color maybe. Yeah, I mean, Kevin would tell you that he could have retitled that book, “Fuck This Guy: A Story of AI CEOs.” They don’t like each other. If you had to relive that moment [of the OpenAI board vote] and say, “I don’t trust Sam,” would you relive that moment? Would you do it the same way? Oh, for sure. I mean, we went into it knowing that it was going to suck. So yeah, for sure. Do you think that these guys are trustworthy? Do you think Sam is trustworthy? I think my stance on that is pretty clear, and I also think that if our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we’re pretty screwed. That’s why I do the work that I do, because I think we need to have different structures and many more people involved with many more perspectives being represented. You have some hindsight now. You knew it was going to suck going into it. You definitely know it sucked coming out of it. What would you have done differently about that time? It’s kind of hard to give the full answer to that because it would take unpicking all this stuff and all these legal restrictions and blah, blah, blah, blah. For sure a thing would have been building stronger relationships with executives on the team. The way that the company related to the board could have been different if more board members had had that. I knew some of the folks pretty well, but that’s one thing. I don’t know. I think we could have… Yeah, no, I think beyond that, it just gets hard to… You have to go in and say, “What were all the different micro decisions and why do we make those decisions and which ones could be—” What is the show? It’s a show about decisions. I’ve got another hour. [Laughs] Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, and then my answers would all get annoying and legal. Fair enough. I’m curious about it because as they go public, there will be market forces acting on them in a totally new way. There will be an investor class. There’ll be an entire CNBC machine that wakes up every day and is like, “Is Anthropic winning or is OpenAI winning?” That is a race dynamic that might be really healthy. It might keep them from trying to kill everyone in the world because they have a bunch of investors looking for their next quarterly earnings, or it might push them further into an unhealthy kind of race. How do you see that playing out, given what you know of these people? It’s going to be really interesting to see if going public is good or bad for their governance. A lot of people are like, “Oh no, going public, there’s going to be so much pressure to make a profit that they’re not going to be able to consider other things.” But at the same time, the corporate governance of public companies is much more structured, much more regulated, and subject to much more external scrutiny than for private companies. I think even things like getting to see Anthropic’s S-1 and thinking, “Okay, what are they doing and why are they doing it? And how do they think about the risks they’re facing, and how do they communicate about those with investors?” Or even things like the Trump administration putting in place this kind of accord , they call it “Super Intelligence,” that several of the leading companies signed. That was structured around, for example, having certain types of things being reported to an independent committee of the board. That idea of an independent committee of the board is kind of toothless if it’s a private company that is deciding on its own. I thought about you when I read that. I was like, “Boy, some independent boards have gotten in a lot of trouble before.” But if it’s a public company, then an independent committee of the board has a pretty strong legal meaning. So I don’t know. It’s something that I’m watching with great interest. The other race dynamic here is China. You mentioned China before. Inside of our country, a bunch of labs are going to go public. They’re going to become some of the richest companies in the history of the world, and they’re going to fight for every dollar that capitalism can generate, and hopefully that restrains them. The market forces will restrain them, and hopefully your work with legislators in this country does something. And then there’s a whole other country that doesn’t listen to us or have anything to do with us, and they’re just going to distill our models and do whatever they want. That is the other argument for not placing any restrictions on these companies that everyone hears all the time. What should I make of that? I’m of two minds about it. How should I think about it? Yeah. I think of this as the ”But China!” argument, which is like, “Well, yeah, we should do this, we should do that, ‘But China!’” I think the way to engage with it is an actual genuine problem that we have to grapple with, and we should be strategic and thoughtful about it and do our best to try and solve it as a problem as opposed to using it as a throwaway excuse. Like, “Oh yeah, sure, sure, sure. All that stuff would be so nice, ‘But China!’, so we’re stuck. There’s nothing we can do.” So what does that look like in practice? If you’re serious about wanting the US to have stronger AI than China, then you need to think really hard about how much US AI development is helping Chinese AI progress. So the one that people talk about all the time, as you mentioned, is distillation, which is, “Are they using US models to generate massive amounts of training data for their own models and therefore progressing faster than they would otherwise?” So certainly I think it makes sense to try and crack down on that and prevent it from happening. But another one, for example, is security and how easy would it be for Chinese actors or other actors, frankly, to steal algorithmic secrets, to steal wholesale model weights. If they can steal the weights of your Astra or your Mythos model and just take them back to their own servers, your lead has vanished. You now have a lead of zero. Right now these companies, especially the smaller ones, but even OpenAI and Anthropic, do not have very good security. We’ve seen both of them over the last few months have external teams manage to hack into spaces that have large amounts of algorithmic secrets. In OpenAI’s case, it was their monorepo and GitHub, which had all of their code. And in Anthropic’s case, I think — and actually maybe the OpenAI case also involved this — the hackers got access to Slack . You’re just going to have so insanely much rich information about how to build better AI if you can get that access. So when our AI gets better, are we actually lengthening our lead or are we just pulling China along with us in these different ways? The other aspect of this is just seriously treating China as an actor in this space and trying to think seriously about their motivations and their likely actions and responses. In my mind, a huge reason that a lot of things are not happening right now is most people are not convinced about this threat model that AI will become the machine god and will take over and humans will all die or will be subservient or whatever. I think it’s fair for people to not be convinced of that, because the evidence is sort of conflicting and unclear, but if that is actually what we think could seriously happen, then China doesn’t want that either. So then it becomes a question of, “Okay, how do we try and get them on the same page of, ‘this threat that we’re worried about is a real threat to worry about?’ Because then they will be making their own decisions in their own self-interest.” I think an approach of, “Well, the US has to force China to do something using some kind of leverage,” is never ever going to work. But an approach of, “Well, look, if we think this is a serious problem that’s going to affect us as humans, and the people in China are also humans, and also if we think this is a problem around who has control, the Chinese Communist Party really, really wants to have control, and so they’re going to have their own incentives and their own decision-making around how to fix that.” Well, let me put it on a spectrum for you. This is very dumb and you’re going to laugh, but just go with me on this. On the one end, it is nuclear weapons and the Chinese government wants a nuclear weapon and they’re going to do whatever they can to control that weapon and they will run their industries differently.  If they get out of line, the CEO of Alibaba goes. He just disappears for a while and then comes back — Chinese government stuff. We need a nuclear weapon, too. If we don’t get there first, then we’ll never get the nonproliferation treaty that we need to keep us all safe for mutually assured destruction. That’s one framework. Way on the other end, I spent five years of my life listening to telecom executives tell me that if we didn’t build 5G networks first, China would get them, and then something . No one could ever tell me what the “something” was. Where on that spectrum between 5G and nuclear weapons is the US-China AI race? I think we need another dimension because in that example, your dimension is significance. But I think the controllability is a huge question as well. So it’s like, what are the examples that people use? Is it a nuclear weapon or is it dragons from House of the Dragon ? Casey Newton had a great Platformer post where he explained he was watching House of the Dragon and thought, “This is what the AI companies are doing. They’re trying to build these things that they think will help them, but actually it’s just going to rain down destruction.” [Laughs] Casey told me he was buying an iPhone Duo so he could watch more TV. He’s a dear friend, but okay. But I think that’s really important because if we think this is a technology we can control, then obviously we want to have the best technology. Obviously, we want to go foot to the floor, get there as fast as we can, and the same is true for China. The question is, if we are not sure if we can control it, then what do we do? Maybe we want to be more cautious and then maybe we want to try and figure out a way to not have China just be overtaking us. But if we’re correct we should be worried about— So that’s nuclear weapons. Well, no, but if it’s dragons, if we’re correct that we need to be worried about whether we can control this, then that’s also something that should be interesting to China. I remember this Casey post, but let me just try to pull this apart so I understand it. The difference between dragons and nuclear weapons is the dragons have some agency, right? They can go away and do bad things on their own. Yes. The dragons might just decide to burn down your whole city. Obviously these are machines — they’re just math, they’re not magical. So instead of dragons, you could think of it as nuclear weapons with faulty control settings, where you build nuclear weapons, but it’s impossible to be sure that it’s not just going to go off and fly to a city and fly to one of your own cities and wipe you out. That’s a very different technology than real nuclear weapons that exist. It is true. No one ever said that about 5G. I’ll be clear about that. The reason I’m asking about this is because those problems do align nation-states, right? We do have nuclear nonproliferation agreements. As you mentioned, there are all kinds of incentives for nation-states to not do cyberattacks willy-nilly because those have real-world consequences. Is there any evidence that these governments have started to align on these problems? Or is it still the pure “But China!” race dynamic? I actually think there is starting to be some early evidence. One way I think about what happened this year in AI from a policy perspective, less than a product or economic perspective, is we saw these two big demonstrations of the two major concerns people have. So the two major concerns are misuse and misalignment, meaning misuse is bad people using AI for bad things and misalignment is AI going rogue or doing things we didn’t want. So this year we had Mythos and we had the Hugging Face attack. Both of those are just really vivid, crisp real-world demonstrations of what these misuse and misalignment concerns could look like. The US and Chinese governments are starting from very different places on AI regulation. They’re both starting from where they started, and what they did with, internet regulation. So the US is starting from a “hands off, laissez-faire, absolutely nothing, do whatever you want” approach. China is starting from a massively locked-down internet with tons of censorship and the Great Firewall. So those are two very different starting points.  I’m not a China expert, but I operate a lot in China circles and I’ve lived in China and so on. But it seems like just over the past even one to three months, starting from those two very different points, they are seeing more in common around threats from major cyberattacks and also threats of loss of control. I’m a language nerd and it’s really interesting tracking the different language China uses about AI. So they’re now talking about loss of control as a thing, but they probably usually don’t mean the same thing that Westerners mean where “loss of control” is like “AI takeover.” They probably mean something more prosaic, but then sometimes they talk about “extreme loss of control,” which maybe is the thing we mean. I do think that there are starting to be some signs of convergence. I think it’ll be a long road. The state of the US-China relationship is such that there’s going to be very, very, very little trust on either side. So I am not optimistic that they’ll just get to sit down in a room and hash out a deal and everything will be great. But I think there is enough space. Basically, if there’s enough shared threat perception, then it might be possible at some point in the future to do something about that. Helen, you’ve given me so much time. As you can tell, I’m just delighted with this conversation. It’s been very fun. We are on the cusp of a new Congress. There are a bunch of new governors. The data center referendums passed overwhelmingly in this country. There’s a new set of regulators in town, right? They’re going to do some stuff. What are some signs people should look for to indicate we’re going to be on the right path and what are some signs that we’re just chasing our tail? Set AI aside, forget about AI. Congress in general is very bad at passing things right now. This is not a this administration thing, this is not an AI thing. So one sign is like, can Congress pass anything? That will be a good sign. It’s also really interesting to look at what state legislatures have been doing in AI. There’s been a lot of concern about the possibility of a state patchwork on AI, with different states passing conflicting things. With the issues that we’ve been talking about today, which I think of as frontier AI risks or the risks from the most advanced systems, there’s actually been a pretty coordinated push in different states. California passed this one bill and then New York passed almost the same bill with just a little more added to it. And then Illinois passed almost the same bill with a little more added to it. I think there’s going to be a lot of momentum over the next year or two to keep building on that at the state level. So that is something that I’ll be watching. Even just specifically California is already looking at how they can strengthen things. So that is something I’ll be looking for. I think honestly, with such a Democratic Congress, I am also concerned that they will overstep here, that they will try and do something that is too sweeping. You had this huge mess in Colorado where they passed this giant AI bill that then was a terrible idea. And so then they had all these committees and follow-up and it was awful. A lot of what we need right now is focused on these frontier systems and the possibility that we have really, really advanced systems in a short amount of time and having much more transparency around that and much clearer standards for how they manage risk. I would not be that excited about an attempt to do a really comprehensive AI regulatory push that covers AI all across the economy and all different kinds of AI systems that are less advanced. There are negative signals that are like “nothing’s going to happen,” and there are negative signals like, “oh, maybe too much is going to happen,” but it’ll be interesting to see where they get to. I suspect we’re going to want to have you back as this Congress starts to get to work and we see some of these ideas. I would love to. I’m eager for your take on it. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thanks so much. This was really fun. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

articles.fullContent: Jensen Huang离开英伟达一事在亚洲引发了各种各样的反应，一些政府正着手确认芯片供应承诺，而另一些政府则在监测此事对本地项目的影响或处理正在进行的调查。 11月8日星期日，有报道称黄仁勋成为中国间谍行动的目标，Nvidia董事会随后启动了独立调查；黄仁勋承认与总部位于新加坡的芯片公司Megaspeed前高管Alice Huang有染。 英伟达的影响力远远超出了美国。 这家芯片巨头与世界各地的公司建立了密切的联系，特别是在亚洲，其许多关键合作伙伴在全球人工智能行业中发挥着重要作用。 11月10日，中国外交部驳斥了有关与英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋有联系的中国女商人是间谍的指控，称这些指控毫无根据，是对北京的抹黑。 周五，一位发言人重申反对扰乱全球供应链的出口管制，并表示该部并不知悉有报道将受限的英伟达芯片与与黄仁勋有关的上海数据中心联系起来。 据路透社报道，黄的离职也给价值超过30亿美元的中国人工智能计算项目带来了不确定性，这些项目依赖于英伟达的受限处理器。 其中许多芯片都受到美国 出口管制，使中国公司难以获得。 据新加坡内政部透露，2025年6月，新加坡当局没收了总部位于新加坡的云计算公司Megaspeed前首席执行官Alice Huang的护照，此举是调查其在服务器采购方面可能存在虚假申报行为的一部分。 新加坡该部委表示，由于Alice Huang不住在新加坡，警方拿走了她的护照，以确保她随时可以接受讯问。 调查的重点是，从新加坡运往马来西亚的服务器后来是否在未妥善申报的情况下被运往其他国家。 据该部称，2026年2月，警方认为证据不足，无法确定Alice Huang犯有与涉嫌虚假申报有关的罪行。 然而，当局表示，她故意提供了关于她在Megaspeed的职务的不实信息。 她被警告并被禁止再次入境新加坡。 她的护照于当月归还。 新加坡还表示，尽管多次要求提供有关美国服务器制造商超微的信息，但从美国当局得到的协助有限。 新加坡内政部表示，其对Megaspeed和另外六名个人的调查仍在进行中。 该部未指明这六名个人，也未具体说明他们在该案中的涉嫌角色。 韩国与英伟达关系密切，主要芯片制造商三星电子和SK海力士在其人工智能处理器所用存储芯片的供应方面发挥着重要作用。

articles.fullContent: 截至周六下午，一份呼吁英伟达（Nvidia）恢复该公司近期被罢免的首席执行官黄仁勋职位的请愿书似乎已吸引了超过11.5万个签名。 该请愿网站表示，签名者包括5,965名英伟达现任员工、1,108名前员工和63,063名股东。 知名支持者包括特斯拉和SpaceX首席执行官埃隆·马斯克、Replit首席执行官Amjad Masad、Epic Games首席执行官蒂姆·斯威尼以及Y Combinator首席执行官Garry Tan。 请愿书指出，签署人“担心Jensen在没有经过有意义的正当程序的情况下被免职”，并要求董事会“在独立调查查明事实真相之前让他复职”。请愿书还呼吁董事会确保公正调查，并向公众提供更多信息。 请愿书指出：“Jensen应享有正当程序，而不是被暴民审判。” 黄仁勋于周四辞职，此前四天，他承认与一名芯片公司高管有染，美国情报部门怀疑该高管是中国间谍。 这位前首席执行官已同意在国会作证，而新闻报道还称，黄仁勋曾多次有婚外情。 英伟达任命首席财务官科莱特·克雷斯（Colette Kress）担任公司临时首席执行官，同时物色永久继任者。 英伟达的股价本周大幅下跌，而黄仁勋的离职预计也将给人工智能行业的融资带来一个巨大的缺口。 每周工作日和周日，您都可以获得TechCrunch的精彩报道。 TechCrunch Mobility是您获取交通运输新闻和见解的首选之地。 初创企业是TechCrunch的核心，因此请每周接收我们最精彩的报道。 为行业领袖提供开启新一天所需的信息。 提交您的电子邮件，即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。

articles.fullContent: 代理管理初创公司LangChain周五宣布，该公司已完成一轮由CapitalG领投的3亿美元C轮融资，估值为30亿美元，参与投资的还有新加坡GIC、DFJ Growth、IVP和Sapphire Ventures等投资者。 这比该公司约一年前在IVP领投下筹集1.25亿美元时的12.5亿美元估值高出一倍多。 LangChain 于 2022 年起步，是一个广受欢迎的开源项目，旨在处理早期 LLM 难以胜任的任务，例如搜索网页、调用 API 和与数据库交互。 随着前沿人工智能实验室推出了如今能够胜任这些任务的工具，LangChain 将工作重点转向了管理人工智能代理。 该公司显然已在这个竞争激烈的领域找到了自己的发展方向，其理念很简单：让企业拥有自己的智能。 这家初创公司源于开源，表示其代理创建和管理软件LangSmith并不像主流云服务提供商或尖端人工智能实验室那样试图将用户锁定在任何特定模型、云或生态系统中。 该公司还承诺，LangSmith将包含代理行为，并且易于使用。 诚然，如今还有许多其他初创公司也在宣传类似的优势，而且表现也不错（新晋公司Mintive就是一个例子）。 然而，LangChain起步较早，目前声称拥有7,000家LangSmith客户，其中包括Harvey、Rippling和Clay等知名初创公司，以及Nvidia、丰田和Salesforce等企业。 每周工作日和周日，您都可以获得TechCrunch的精彩报道。 TechCrunch Mobility是您获取交通运输新闻和见解的理想之地。 初创企业是TechCrunch的核心，因此请每周接收我们最精彩的报道。 为有影响力的人物提供他们开始新一天所需的信息。 提交您的电子邮件，即表示您同意我们的条款和隐私声明。

articles.fullContent: OpenAI表示，用户对购买行为拥有完全的掌控权，因为在结账之前，他们可以查看商品、总价以及用于完成交易的支付卡。 此外，用户将通过面容识别或指纹等安全验证直接批准购买，从而生成交易记录。 此次新增功能正值面向消费者的AI工具正努力寻找合适的产品与市场契合点，即如何帮助人们更高效地完成各种任务。 虽然DoorDash和Uber等公司迄今为止报告的人工智能代理下单数量很少，但Meta的Muse目前拥有超过1000万用户，人工智能辅助购物已成为其应用程序上的热门活动。 其他个人人工智能代理，如Instinct，也支持代用户购物。 因此，OpenAI 希望通过自己的代理购物功能进一步进入这一领域也就不足为奇了。 OpenAI 表示，商家将自动从 dot 处收到履行订单所需的信息，例如收货地址和联系方式。 该公司指出，通过dots购物的顾客仍将能够获得信用卡奖励，并能够享受通常随信用卡提供的保障，例如能够对交易提出异议。 上线时有限的可用性将使OpenAI能够在更广泛地推出该功能之前对其进行测试和改进。 未来，该公司计划允许用户设置消费限额，或针对购买类别或时间段配置其他参数，从而为用户提供对该功能的更多控制权，这样用户就可以预先批准购买，然后由代理更自主地处理。 该公司还计划将代理购物功能扩展至更多支持的零售商。 在某些地区，这可能是一个挑战，因为零售商正在阻止 AI 代理使用他们的网站；在购物领域，禁止 AI 代理的最大零售商是亚马逊，因为它希望引导用户使用自己的 AI 代理 Alexa。 为了帮助零售商适应代理式商务，OpenAI 还发布了《商务合作伙伴手册》，为希望支持使用代理的客户的网站提供工具和指导。 当您通过我们文章中的链接进行购买时，我们可能会赚取少量佣金。 这不会影响我们的编辑独立性。 正在发酵的黄仁勋丑闻：时间线Amanda Silberling微软最近的电子邮件服务中断演变为一场全面的全球云端危机Zack Whittaker路透社报道称，黄仁勋有第三段婚外情Russell Brandom

Claude Duet is Anthropic's AI agent for consumers, the latest attempt by an AI company to try to convince us that agents can be useful for people who don't write code. articles.rawFullText: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers.  The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. Foster told MIT Technology Review he intends to introduce new, stricter legislation in the new year that would offer a workaround. The new rule would require licenses to operate advanced GPUs, and before a GPU could connect, its valid license would need to be verified.   In the meantime, the controversy at Nvidia, Foster says, has fueled support among his colleagues for the rules in the bill: “There will be a lot of political pressure, in the wake of everything that’s happened, on the companies to actually do a very good job of the geographic validation of where the chip actually is.”

articles.fullContent: 随着公司希望通过人工智能、云计算和高级建模加速创新，主要挑战是将新技术与可靠的数据、科学专业知识以及将产品推向市场的实际现实联系起来。 对于特种化学品制造商路博润来说，数字化转型就是为研究人员提供更快地测试创意的工具，做出更明智的决策，并在不影响性能的情况下开发更可持续的材料。 路博润信息技术副总裁Girish Rao表示，该公司正在建立一个数字基础，将业务流程、现代数据平台和云基础设施连接起来，以支持其研发(R&D)团队。他们的目标是将数十年积累的技术数据与了解客户需求以及工作物理限制的化学家和工程师的深厚专业知识相结合。 数据科学家可以帮助识别模式，测试新的假设，并在研究人员进行物理实验之前对可能性进行建模。但是， Rao强调， “这不是要取代科学判断，而是要为我们的科学家提供更好的工具。“科学家、数据科学家和IT团队从不同的角度处理问题，分别优先考虑实验有效性、模型性能、平台安全性和可扩展性。 通过将这些团队聚集在“融合团队”中，路博润将他们围绕共同的目标进行协调，从建立信任的小型试点开始。Rao说： “一旦团队成员之间建立了信任，他们就知道自己将要创造什么样的价值。” “云基础设施还为公司提供了访问计算资源和现代工具的灵活性，而无需进行建设和维护自己的数据中心所需的大量投资。事实证明，这些能力在推进可持续发展方面尤其有价值。 数字建模可以帮助研究人员评估更多配方，探索淀粉和玉米基替代品等材料，并评估产品生命周期中的权衡。在实验室中承诺材料只是第一步。 在满足绩效预期、监管要求和财务限制的同时扩展生产仍然是一条钢丝绳，但人工智能对多个变量进行建模的能力可以帮助团队应对这些相互竞争的需求。展望未来，随着实验室变得更加智能化，制造工厂变得更加高效， Rao预计人工智能、自动化、高级建模、数字孪生和互联数据将融合在一起。

articles.rawFullText: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid.  One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport .  Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out.  Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me, industry insiders see their ambitions as constrained less by public opposition than by a lack of electricity. That should tell us something. So what happens next? It’s possible that newly elected politicians’ actual stances on data centers won’t be as negative as the ones they campaigned on. But what seems true regardless is that if new data centers need their own power generated onsite, they’ll go where there are the fewest people able to resist them. That might mean the Permian Basin , where a network of natural-gas lines can be easy for developers to connect to and populations are sparse. Companies might also try their chances abroad; Google, in fact, announced the day after the elections that it will spend $15 billion on data center projects in Malaysia. But there’s one place where Big Tech may find virtually no limits at all, as Elon Musk posted just hours after the midterms results came rolling in: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.rawFullText: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy.  I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation.  Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth.  “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator.  He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides  some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. And I hope if that’s what it does take—which, like I said, I hope it doesn’t—but if it does, I hope it’s as small as possible.”

articles.rawFullText: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons , even if just for an hour. I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round. Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.  But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors. With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there. But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide. The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing. When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said. Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.) You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger. In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle. The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out. Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.  But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care. Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.

articles.rawFullText: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem. Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows. articles.rawFullText: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail. Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.  Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.  The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium. That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.  The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects. Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it. A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.  It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.  This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.  Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

articles.originalTitle: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
